In adults and children presenting with signs and symptoms of extrapulmonary tuberculosis (TB), the use of Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra is recommended for detecting rifampicin resistance, rather than relying on culture and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST). This recommendation is strong for Xpert MTB/RIF due to high certainty of evidence for test accuracy, but evidence for Xpert Ultra is of low certainty. 2. In HIV-positive adults and children with signs and symptoms of disseminated TB, Xpert MTB/RIF may be used on blood samples as an initial diagnostic test for disseminated TB. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 3. In children with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB in settings where the pretest probability is below 5% and the initial Xpert MTB/RIF test result is negative, repeated testing with Xpert MTB/RIF using sputum, gastric fluid, nasopharyngeal aspirate, or stool specimens is not recommended. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence for sputum test accuracy and very low certainty for other specimen types. 4. In children with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB in settings where the pretest probability is 5% or higher and the initial Xpert MTB/RIF test result is negative, a second Xpert MTB/RIF test (for a total of two tests) using sputum, gastric fluid, nasopharyngeal aspirate, or stool specimens may be used. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence for sputum test accuracy and very low certainty for other specimen types. 5. In children with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB in settings where the pretest probability is below 5% and the initial Xpert Ultra test result is negative, repeated testing with Xpert Ultra using sputum or nasopharyngeal aspirate specimens is not recommended. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 6. In children with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB in settings where the pretest probability is 5% or higher and the initial Xpert Ultra test result is negative, a second Xpert Ultra test (for a total of two tests) using sputum and nasopharyngeal aspirate specimens may be used. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 7. In adults and children with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB, the Truenat MTB or MTB Plus test may be used as an initial diagnostic test for TB instead of smear microscopy or culture. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 8. In adults and children with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB and a positive Truenat MTB or MTB Plus result, the Truenat MTB-RIF Dx test may be used as an initial test for detecting rifampicin resistance instead of culture and phenotypic DST. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 9. In HIV-positive children, adolescents, and adults, the LF-LAM test is recommended to assist in diagnosing active TB in the following scenarios: In inpatient settings for individuals with signs and symptoms of TB (pulmonary and/or extrapulmonary) (strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). In individuals with advanced HIV disease or those who are seriously ill (strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). Regardless of TB symptoms, in individuals with a CD4 cell count below 200 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). 10. In outpatient settings, the LF-LAM test is conditionally recommended for individuals with signs and symptoms of TB (pulmonary and/or extrapulmonary) or those who are seriously ill, with low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. It is also conditionally recommended for individuals with a CD4 cell count below 100 cells/mm³, regardless of TB symptoms, with very low certainty of evidence for test accuracy. 11. Xpert MTB/RIF may replace conventional microscopy, culture, and histopathology for testing non-respiratory specimens (e.g., lymph nodes and other tissues) in children suspected of having extrapulmonary TB. This is a conditional recommendation with very low quality of evidence. 12. Xpert MTB/RIF should be used instead of conventional microscopy and culture as the initial diagnostic test for cerebrospinal fluid specimens in children suspected of having TB meningitis. This is a strong recommendation due to the urgency of rapid diagnosis, despite very low quality of evidence. 13. Chest radiography is a useful diagnostic tool for pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB in children when combined with clinical history, evidence of TB infection, and microbiological testing. 14. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all individuals, including children, with presumptive or diagnosed TB. This is a strong recommendation with low quality of evidence. 15. Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis in low HIV prevalence settings and/or low isoniazid resistance prevalence, as well as HIV-negative children, can be treated with a three-drug regimen (HRZ) for two months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for four months. This is a strong recommendation with moderate quality of evidence. 16. Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or TB peripheral lymphadenitis, or those with extensive pulmonary disease in high HIV prevalence settings and/or high isoniazid resistance prevalence, should be treated with a four-drug regimen (HRZE) for two months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for four months. This is a strong recommendation with moderate quality of evidence. 17. Infants aged 0–3 months with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis should be promptly treated with standard regimens, with potential dose adjustments to account for age and toxicity. Dose adjustments should be made by clinicians experienced in managing pediatric TB. This is a strong recommendation with low quality of evidence. 18. Streptomycin should not be used as part of first-line treatment regimens for children with pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis. This is a strong recommendation with moderate quality of evidence. 19. Children with suspected or confirmed tuberculous meningitis or osteoarticular TB should be treated with a four-drug regimen (HRZE) for two months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for 10 months, for a total treatment duration of 12 months. 20. In countries with high TB or leprosy incidence, a single dose of the BCG vaccine should be given to all healthy neonates at birth to prevent TB and leprosy. If not given at birth, it should be administered at the earliest opportunity to protect the child before exposure to infection. 21. In low TB or leprosy incidence countries, selective BCG vaccination may be considered for high-risk groups, such as neonates born to parents with current or previous TB or leprosy, or those in households with contacts to high-incidence countries. 22. Revaccination with BCG is not recommended, even if the TST or IGRA result is negative. The absence of a BCG scar does not indicate a lack of protection and is not a reason for revaccination. 23. Infants exposed to immunosuppressive treatments in utero or via breastfeeding should not receive BCG vaccination. 24. People living with HIV, including children, should not receive BCG vaccination unless they are on ART, clinically well, and immunologically stable (CD4% > 25% for children aged 5 years). 25. In high HIV prevalence populations, BCG vaccination is recommended for neonates born to women of unknown HIV status or neonates of unknown HIV status born to HIV-infected women, provided there is no clinical evidence of HIV infection. 26. Asymptomatic neonates born to mothers with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB should receive TPT if TB disease is excluded and should be followed regularly to confirm the absence of TB. If asymptomatic and HIV-negative at the end of TPT, BCG vaccination should be provided. 27. Infants and children living with HIV who are in contact with a person with TB and are unlikely to have active TB should receive TPT. 28. Children aged ≥12 months living with HIV in high TB transmission settings should be offered TPT as part of comprehensive HIV prevention and care, regardless of TB contact. 29. Children living with HIV who have completed TB treatment may receive TPT. 30. Children aged <5 years who are household contacts of people with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and are found not to have active TB should be given TPT, even if LTBI testing is unavailable. 31. Children aged ≥5 years, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts of people with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and are found not to have active TB may be given TPT. 32. Infants and children living with HIV who have poor weight gain, fever, or cough, or a history of TB contact, should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If TB is excluded, they should be offered TPT regardless of age. 33. The absence of TB symptoms and normal chest radiographic findings may be used to rule out active TB disease in HIV-negative household contacts aged ≥5 years before preventive treatment. 34. Either TST or IGRA can be used to test for LTBI. 35. Recommended LTBI treatment options include 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. Alternatives include a 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or 4 months of daily rifampicin alone. 36. In high TB transmission settings, adults and adolescents living with HIV with unknown or positive LTBI tests and unlikely to have active TB should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT), regardless of ART status, degree of immunosuppression, or pregnancy. 37. TB among pregnant women is associated with increased risks of perinatal death, premature birth, and low birth weight. HIV coinfection further increases maternal and infant mortality risks. TB treatment should begin promptly when its probability is moderate to high. 38. Systematic screening for active TB should be considered for pregnant women as part of antenatal care. Diagnosis and treatment should be promptly provided when TB is suspected. 39. TB diagnosis in pregnant women follows the same protocols as for other adults. TST is safe, and chest radiography can be performed with appropriate shielding to minimize fetal radiation exposure. 40. Most TB medicines are safe during pregnancy, but some, such as amikacin, streptomycin, ethionamide, and prothionamide, are contraindicated. Treatment of drug-resistant TB in pregnant women should be individualized and managed by specialized services with counseling on potential fetal risks. 41. After delivery, breastfeeding should not be discouraged, as the concentration of TB drugs in breast milk is too low to harm the nursing newborn.
